Key Takeaways

NuScale Power (SMR) fell 39% in the month through October 22, closing at $5.38, while Oklo (OKLO) declined 33% and the Nasdaq 100 lost 6%.

Rising Treasury yields and concerns about nuclear project timelines pressured both stocks, with NuScale facing additional uncertainty over its proposed Tennessee Valley Authority project.

Wall Street's average NuScale price target dropped from about $41 to $11 over the past year as analysts grew increasingly cautious about commercial execution.

NuScale's November 5 earnings call could provide an important update, but securing a definitive customer agreement remains a key catalyst.

What Happened?

NuScale Power (SMR:NYSE) stock plunged 39% in the month through October 22, closing at $5.38 as concerns about nuclear project timelines, financing costs, and commercial agreements pressured shares.

Oklo (OKLO:NYSE) declined 33% over the same period, while the Nasdaq 100 fell 6%, highlighting broader weakness among advanced nuclear developers.

Jim Cramer, host of CNBC's Mad Money, captured the shift in sentiment on October 1, saying, "Fermi marked the top for all sorts of long shot nuclear energy companies."

Selling intensified on October 12 as investors questioned whether nuclear developers could turn ambitious project announcements into revenue-generating operations.

On October 14, hotter-than-expected September inflation pushed the 10-year Treasury yield to 5.26%. NuScale fell 10% that session, compared with an 8.6% decline for Oklo, as higher yields weighed on companies whose profits remain years away.

Analysts also became increasingly cautious about NuScale.

UBS downgraded the stock to Sell in September, lowering its target to $6 from $10, while RBC reduced its target to $7 from $10 in October.

Barclays followed on October 20, downgrading NuScale to Underweight and cutting its target to $5 from $11, citing commercial delays and contract uncertainty. Citi subsequently lowered its target to $4, while Truist reduced its forecast to $8.

These reductions coincided with a decline in Wall Street's average price target from $40.84 a year earlier to $11.07 as of October 22.

NuScale Power (SMR): analysts' consensus (mean) price target, $ per share, last year (TIKR)
Why NuScale Faces Greater Uncertainty Than Oklo

Both companies face lengthy development timelines, but Oklo has achieved a meaningful operational milestone that distinguishes its progress.

In August, Oklo's Groves Isotope Test Reactor reached first criticality, establishing a controlled nuclear chain reaction less than a year after groundbreaking. Although it is not a commercial electricity plant, the achievement demonstrated progress toward deployment.

SK hynix Just Dropped 33% in a Month. Is It Time to Sell, or Load Up? ©@Syda Productions via Canva; @IncrediVFX from Getty Images via Canva
Key Takeaways

SK hynix (SKHY) fell 33% in the month through October 22, compared with a 22% decline for Micron (MU) and a 6% drop in the Nasdaq 100.

Lam Research (LRCX) added pressure to semiconductor stocks as investors questioned whether AI infrastructure spending could sustain its rapid growth.

SK hynix reported record Q3 revenue of KRW 104.6 trillion, up 328% year over year, with an 80% operating margin.

Strong HBM demand, long-term customer agreements, and approximately KRW 100 trillion in planned shareholder returns strengthen the case for buying rather than selling.

What Happened?

SK hynix (SKHY:NASDAQ) stock plunged 33% in the month through October 22, closing at $132 as concerns about Chinese memory competition and AI infrastructure spending weighed on semiconductor stocks.

The decline significantly exceeded the broader market's losses. Micron (MU:NASDAQ) fell 22% over the same period, while the Nasdaq 100 declined 6%, highlighting the pressure on memory stocks.

On October 13, China's CXMT reportedly made progress developing denser DRAM technology, raising concerns that expanding Chinese production could eventually pressure memory prices. The company's technological claims have not been independently verified.

Meanwhile, Lam Research (LRCX:NASDAQ) reported September-quarter revenue of $8.22 billion and projected approximately $8.6 billion for the December quarter. Although its outlook indicated continued growth, investors questioned whether semiconductor equipment spending could maintain its recent momentum.

Together, these developments fueled concerns about the sustainability of the memory industry's extraordinary profitability.

However, SK hynix's October 28 earnings challenged the bearish narrative. Shares rebounded following the announcement but closed October 30 at $149, remaining 24% below their September 22 closing price.

Record Earnings Strengthen the Bull Case

SK hynix reported record third-quarter revenue of KRW 104.6 trillion, up 328% year over year and 32% from the previous quarter.

Operating profit reached KRW 83.3 trillion, up 632% year over year, while operating margin climbed to 80% from 76% in the second quarter.

Growth was supported by strong demand for high-bandwidth memory (HBM), advanced server DRAM, and enterprise storage products benefiting from AI infrastructure investment.

Management also confirmed long-term agreements with 14 major customers, covering more than half of expected production capacity for 2027 and 2028.

CEO Kwak Noh-Jung said customer trust built through the company's technological competitiveness is "leading to long-term contracts," providing greater visibility into future demand.

Investors have spent months fixated on megacap tech capex, yet the quiet enablers of that AI buildout sit in global finance. When hyperscalers commit tens of billions to data centers, someone structures the loans, underwrites the bonds, and insures the risks. If the Nasdaq 100 selloff has you questioning where the more predictable cash flows might sit, this piece walks through three large financial intermediaries tied to that story and how the latest AI capex worries may matter for their stocks.

The three stocks covered below are just a small sample, and the full screen surfaced 48 more large financial intermediaries with equally compelling AI capex financing narratives that are not discussed in this article. Derwent London (LSE:DLN)

Derwent London links the AI capex story back to bricks and mortar, offering central London space that can flex between high end offices and edge infrastructure for data heavy tenants.

Derwent London runs a £5.0b central London office portfolio, drawing about £209 million from offices within £412 million of total segment income and a smaller contribution from trading property sales and service charges, off a roughly £2.1b market cap.

A structurally higher occupier focus on offices as a strategic tool for culture and talent attraction, combined with Derwent London's design led, amenity rich product and clustering model, is expected to support leasing spreads and net operating margins.

What really moves the dial is how one pressure on future tenant demand plays out against that carefully curated London footprint.

How that demand pressure plays against Derwent London's curated footprint is exactly what the full narrative for Derwent London unpacks, including where AI linked occupier demand could be accelerating.

LSE:DLN Earnings & Revenue History as at Nov 2026
MERLIN Properties SOCIMI (BME:MRL)

MERLIN Properties SOCIMI is an Iberian commercial landlord connected to the AI capex buildout, owning offices, malls, logistics and data centre assets. Revenue primarily comes from office buildings at about €295 million, with shopping centers at €132 million, logistics at €83 million and data centers at €71 million, supporting a roughly €7.1b market cap.

MERLIN Properties SOCIMI provides exposure to AI-driven data-center and logistics demand through rent and asset ownership rather than direct tech project risk. As hyperscalers reassess heavy capex, a key issue is how that pressure may influence lease terms and pricing power on its power-intensive sites.

The Nasdaq-100 spent part of Friday, October 30, 2026, below the line that defines a correction, then climbed back above it before the close. It fell 3.46% to close at 28,384.85, after reaching an intraday low of 28,093.24.

Who is Danny / Shutterstock.com

That low sat 10.0% below the October 6 record close of 31,224.47. A correction means a 10% drop from a record, so the index crossed that line during the session. It closed 9.1% below the record, which means it never finished a day in correction.

Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) closed at $690.49, down 3.47%. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86% to 25,437.00, its lowest close since July 31.

The selling started in chips. Shares of Intel (NASDAQ:INTC) fell 28.6% after it guided fourth-quarter revenue to $15 billion to $16 billion, below the $16.5 billion it had just reported. Joe Tigay, a portfolio manager at Equity Armor Investments, said, "We're moving out of the hopes and dreams phase of the AI trade and into the 'show me' phase."

Why the Close Matters More Than the Intraday Low

The correction label is based on closing prices, and buyers came in before the close and raised the index back above the line. Volatility followed the same path. The VIX, which measures how much investors expect the S&P 500 to swing, hit 23.93 during the session but closed at 19.41, up 12.91%.

American sovereign debt surged during the week through Oct. 30, driven by a sharp pullback in tech shares linked to artificial intelligence and expanding corporate credit risk spreads that accelerated safe-haven flows into Treasuries.

Primary revenue channels for major American tech giants are demonstrating initial signs of cooling, even as total corporate artificial intelligence investments approach the $750 billion mark for the year. Meanwhile, costs to protect the debt of numerous U.S. technology heavyweights against default hit fresh record highs Friday. The protection price for Intel bonds for five years surged as much as 22.4 basis points Friday morning to 127.9 basis points a year, Bloomberg reported.

The benchmark 10-year Treasury yield remained below the 5.00% threshold for the second straight week. The 30-year U.S. Treasury yield remained largely unchanged at 5.31% for the week ending Oct. 30.

The spread between the U.S. 10-year yield and the U.S. 2-year yield ticked marginally higher by 3 basis points to 0.33% in the week.

The iShares 20+ Year Treasury ETF (TLT) ended the week 0.6% higher, its fourth straight week of gains, while the shorter-duration iShares 1-3 year ETF (SHY) added about 0.3%. The slight recovery in the shorter-duration bond ETF may reflect easing short-term inflation pressure; however, markets still factor in one more rate hike in December.

US stocks fell sharply on Friday after Intel and Amazon fell on disappointing earnings reports released Thursday afternoon. Further AI worries emerged after the Financial Times reported Friday that Blackstone told investors Anthropic may not receive an investment-grade credit rating immediately after going public. Chip stocks saw heavy losses, led by a -28% plunge in Intel. Higher oil prices also hurt stocks.

Market sentiment was also hurt by news of a $6.3 billion heist at the Binance exchange, which led to heavy losses in crypto stocks.

The Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by less than the S&P 500 or Nasdaq 100, as 12 of the 30 stocks closed higher. Some large-cap consumer, pharma, and oil stocks saw some defensive buying as investors rotated out of tech stocks.

Crypto-exchange Binance has frozen all withdrawals until possibly Sunday after a $6.3 billion heist on Thursday. Binance said it would reimburse customers for losses. The exchange holds some $135 billion of assets. North Korean hackers were blamed for the incident. Bitcoin on Friday fell by more than -2%, adding to Thursday's loss of -3% on the initial news of the Binance heist.

Dec WTI crude oil prices rallied +2.1% on Friday as the market faces the possibility of a US military strike on Iran as soon as next week, after Tuesday's (Nov 3) US mid-term elections. The Wall Street Journal reported Thursday that a top US commander has briefed President Trump on his military options. Meanwhile, European diesel futures rose on a report that Ukraine hit a refinery in Russia's Samara region. Reports also cited two attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

Stocks are supported by the prospect of solid quarterly earnings. According to data compiled by Bloomberg Intelligence, Q3 S&P 500 earnings are expected to climb by +31% from a year earlier, up from a July estimate of 22%. As of Thursday, 286 of the S&P 500 companies have reported results, with 82% beating estimates.
